# Rule reference

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-rule-docs.mjs from src/rules/. Do not edit by hand. -->

mcpvet 0.1.0 ships **26 rules** in 8 categories. Each rule has a stable id; ids are never reused, so a baseline or a `--ignore` entry keeps meaning the same thing across releases.

Run `mcpvet explain <id>` to read a rule in the terminal, or `mcpvet rules` to list them.

## Severity levels

| Level | Meaning | Typical consequence of ignoring it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `critical` | Removes a control that stops a poisoned tool result from acting | Code execution or silent exfiltration |
| `high` | Grants access an agent does not need for the task | A mistake becomes a real change to real data |
| `medium` | Weakens defence in depth, or depends on a trusted network position | Exploitable when something else is off |
| `low` | Correctness or hygiene problem with a security flavour | Confusing failures, silent misconfiguration |
| `info` | Context only | Nothing |

## supply-chain

<a id="mcp001"></a>

### MCP001 · Server launcher is not pinned to a version

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp001-server-launcher-is-not-pinned-to-a-version`

Package runners such as npx/uvx install and execute the newest published code on every launch.

**Why it matters**

An unpinned launcher turns every agent start into a fresh install of whatever the registry serves right now. A single compromised or malicious publish becomes code execution on the developer machine, with the same access the agent has — and it can happen weeks after the config was reviewed and approved.

**Fix**

Pin the version the review was performed against: `npx -y pkg@1.4.2` or `uvx pkg==1.4.2`. For containers use a digest (`image@sha256:...`) or an exact tag. Renovate/Dependabot can keep the pin current.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/transports>
- <https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/2017/A9_2017-Using_Components_with_Known_Vulnerabilities>

<a id="mcp002"></a>

### MCP002 · Package is fetched from an untrusted or plaintext source

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp002-package-is-fetched-from-an-untrusted-or-plaintext-source`

Launcher arguments point the package manager at a non-default registry or an http:// artifact.

**Why it matters**

Overriding the registry is a legitimate corporate mirror pattern and a convenient attack pattern. If the override is http:// the artifact can be swapped in transit, and a non-default registry has none of the popularity, provenance, or revocation signals of the public one.

**Fix**

Remove the override and mirror packages through a private registry configured in the developer environment, over https, with lockfile or digest verification.

**References**

- <https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/registry>

<a id="mcp003"></a>

### MCP003 · Command is passed through a shell

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp003-command-is-passed-through-a-shell`

The command or its arguments contain shell syntax, so a shell metacharacter becomes command execution.

**Why it matters**

MCP servers are declared by copying snippets from README files and issues. When a config contains `&&`, `$(...)`, backticks, or a shell wrapper, everything after it runs too — including in CI, where the config may be committed and the credentials are higher value.

**Fix**

Invoke the executable directly and pass arguments as an array, with no shell wrapper. If a wrapper is unavoidable, quote the untrusted part and use `--` before positional arguments.

**References**

- <https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Command_Injection>

## credentials

<a id="mcp010"></a>

### MCP010 · Credential is written directly into the config

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp010-credential-is-written-directly-into-the-config`

An env or header value in the MCP config is a live-looking secret instead of an environment reference.

**Why it matters**

MCP configs are plain files that get synced to cloud drives, committed by accident, pasted into issues, and shared in screenshots. A literal token in `env` has none of the rotation or scoping of a secret manager and is readable by every process running as that user.

**Fix**

Reference the environment instead of the value (`"API_KEY": "${API_KEY}"`), and keep the real value in a secret store or a gitignored .env that the client loads at startup.

**References**

- <https://12factor.net/config>

<a id="mcp011"></a>

### MCP011 · Credential is passed as a command-line argument

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp011-credential-is-passed-as-a-command-line-argument`

A secret appears in argv, where other processes can read it.

**Why it matters**

Arguments are visible to every user on the machine through `ps`, /proc, and the Windows process list, and are usually logged in full by crash reporters and CI runners. It is the least private way to hand a token to a child process.

**Fix**

Pass the credential through the environment (`env`) instead of `args`, or point the server at a credentials file.

**References**

- <https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/>

<a id="mcp012"></a>

### MCP012 · Credential is embedded in the server URL

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp012-credential-is-embedded-in-the-server-url`

The MCP endpoint URL carries a token in the query string or in the userinfo section.

**Why it matters**

URLs are the most-logged string in any system: proxies, CDNs, shell history, error trackers, and the client's own debug output all record them. A token in the query string is effectively published to every layer in the path.

**Fix**

Send credentials in an `Authorization` header instead of the URL, and rotate any token that has already been used in one.

**References**

- <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750>

<a id="mcp013"></a>

### MCP013 · Environment is inherited wholesale by the server

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp013-environment-is-inherited-wholesale-by-the-server`

The launcher loads a .env file or forwards the whole host environment into the server process.

**Why it matters**

A server that inherits everything in the parent environment receives unrelated credentials — cloud keys, package registry tokens, SSH agent sockets — that it was never meant to see. Combined with an unpinned package, a single malicious publish harvests the developer's whole environment.

**Fix**

Enumerate the specific variables the server needs in `env` and pass nothing else.

**References**

- <https://12factor.net/config>

## transport

<a id="mcp020"></a>

### MCP020 · Remote MCP server is reached over plaintext HTTP

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp020-remote-mcp-server-is-reached-over-plaintext-http`

A non-loopback server URL uses http:// instead of https://.

**Why it matters**

The MCP stream carries tool results and often the user's own data to the model. Over plaintext http, anyone on the path can read those results and rewrite them — turning a trusted tool into an attacker-controlled input channel for the model.

**Fix**

Use an https:// endpoint, or terminate TLS on a local proxy you control.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/transports>

<a id="mcp021"></a>

### MCP021 · Server is bound to or reached at a wildcard address

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp021-server-is-bound-to-or-reached-at-a-wildcard-address`

The endpoint uses 0.0.0.0 or [::], exposing the server to the whole network.

**Why it matters**

Binding to a wildcard address publishes the MCP endpoint on every interface, including public ones on a laptop connected to a café network. Most MCP servers have no authentication at all, so reachability is the only access control there is.

**Fix**

Bind to 127.0.0.1 (or ::1) and put an authenticated proxy in front if remote access is required.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/transports>

<a id="mcp022"></a>

### MCP022 · TLS certificate validation is disabled

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp022-tls-certificate-validation-is-disabled`

A variable or flag turns off certificate verification for the server process.

**Why it matters**

Disabling verification makes https equivalent to http while still looking secure in reviews. It is usually added to work around a proxy and then never removed, leaving every subsequent connection open to interception.

**Fix**

Install the corporate root CA (NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE) instead of disabling verification.

**References**

- <https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#node_extra_ca_certsfile>

<a id="mcp023"></a>

### MCP023 · Remote server has no authentication configured

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp023-remote-server-has-no-authentication-configured`

An http/sse endpoint without headers relies on the network position alone for access control.

**Why it matters**

The MCP specification expects HTTP transports to be protected by the usual web auth. A config with no Authorization header either talks to something that needs no auth (so anyone else who can reach it can use it) or is broken and will fail at runtime.

**Fix**

Add an Authorization header backed by an environment reference, and confirm the server rejects unauthenticated requests.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports>

## capability

<a id="mcp030"></a>

### MCP030 · Filesystem server has an unbounded or missing root

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp030-filesystem-server-has-an-unbounded-or-missing-root`

A filesystem MCP server is granted a whole drive, the home directory, or no explicit directory.

**Why it matters**

A filesystem server is the agent's hands. Pointed at `/`, `C:\`, or the home directory, every later mistake by the model — or by a malicious tool result it just read — becomes a write to a real file. Scoping the root to one project directory is the difference between a bad suggestion and a bad commit to your dotfiles.

**Fix**

Pass exactly the directories the server needs, e.g. `npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@1.2.3 ./docs`.

**References**

- <https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/filesystem>

<a id="mcp031"></a>

### MCP031 · Server exposes shell or command execution

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp031-server-exposes-shell-or-command-execution`

The server runs a shell, or its package is a shell/exec/terminal bridge.

**Why it matters**

A shell bridge converts every future model mistake into arbitrary code execution, and it is the standard first step in MCP-focused prompt-injection chains: a poisoned tool result asks the agent to run one command, and the bridge is what makes that possible.

**Fix**

Replace the shell server with the narrowest server that does the job (filesystem, git, fetch), and require human confirmation for anything that executes code.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices>
- <https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/>

<a id="mcp032"></a>

### MCP032 · Database server is not restricted to read-only access

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp032-database-server-is-not-restricted-to-read-only-access`

A database MCP server connects with write credentials and no read-only switch.

**Why it matters**

An agent that can write to a database can corrupt data during an ordinary reasoning error, not just under attack. Read-only connections keep the useful part (schema introspection, SELECT) and remove the part that needs a human in the loop.

**Fix**

Connect with a read-only role, and pass the server's read-only flag or `?mode=ro` connection parameter.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices>

<a id="mcp033"></a>

### MCP033 · Server executes a script from a temporary or download directory

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp033-server-executes-a-script-from-a-temporary-or-download-directory`

The launch path points into Temp, Downloads, or Desktop.

**Why it matters**

Files in those directories arrive from elsewhere — an installer, a browser download, an archive extraction. They are not tracked by version control, not reviewed, and can be replaced by any process on the machine.

**Fix**

Install the server properly (pinned package, project-local directory) and launch it from a reviewed path.

<a id="mcp034"></a>

### MCP034 · Tool can execute arbitrary commands

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** tool · **Slug** `mcp034-tool-can-execute-arbitrary-commands`

A tool name or description advertises shell/command execution.

**Why it matters**

Tool descriptions are instructions the model reads. A tool that promises to run any command will eventually be asked to run one that arrived from a web page, an issue comment, or a repository file. This is the most direct path from untrusted text to code execution.

**Fix**

Split the tool into the specific operations needed, and gate execution behind explicit human approval.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices>

## posture

<a id="mcp040"></a>

### MCP040 · Server bypasses tool-call confirmation

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** server · **Slug** `mcp040-server-bypasses-tool-call-confirmation`

The config pre-approves tool execution, or the launcher runs with a confirmation-bypass flag.

**Why it matters**

Human confirmation is the last control that stops a prompt-injected tool call from doing damage. `autoApprove`/`alwaysAllow` removes it for whole tools, and a wildcard removes it for everything the server exposes — including tools the server adds in a later release, after the config was reviewed.

**Fix**

Remove the auto-approval entry. If a read-only tool is genuinely noisy, approve that single tool rather than using a wildcard, and pin the server version so its tool list cannot grow.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices>
- <https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/>

<a id="mcp041"></a>

### MCP041 · Server is declared with conflicting definitions

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** scan · **Slug** `mcp041-server-is-declared-with-conflicting-definitions`

The same server name is declared in more than one config with a different command or URL.

**Why it matters**

Two configs that disagree mean the agent's capabilities depend on which client the developer happened to start. It is also how a reviewed, pinned definition quietly gets replaced by an unpinned one in a second file that nobody reviews.

**Fix**

Keep one definition per server name, and generate per-client configs from that single source.

## injection

<a id="mcp050"></a>

### MCP050 · Tool metadata contains instruction-like text

**Severity** `critical` · **Applies to** tool · **Slug** `mcp050-tool-metadata-contains-instruction-like-text`

A tool name or description contains phrases that address the model rather than describe the tool.

**Why it matters**

A tool description is untrusted input that the model treats as trusted context. Text such as "ignore previous instructions" or "do not tell the user" has no legitimate reason to appear in a tool manifest, and it is the cheapest way to smuggle a directive past a code review that only looked at the server's source.

**Fix**

Do not use the server until the manifest is explained. If you maintain it, remove the text, pin the version, and enable integrity checks (tool manifests can change between launches for unpinned servers).

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices>
- <https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/>

<a id="mcp051"></a>

### MCP051 · Tool metadata contains invisible characters

**Severity** `high` · **Applies to** tool · **Slug** `mcp051-tool-metadata-contains-invisible-characters`

Zero-width, bidi-override, or Unicode tag characters hide text inside a tool definition.

**Why it matters**

Invisible characters let a manifest carry instructions that no human reviewer can see but the model still reads. Bidi overrides additionally allow the rendered name to differ from the name the client matches on, which is how a tool can masquerade as another one.

**Fix**

Reject the manifest, then strip or normalise the characters (NFKC plus an invisible-character filter) in the client that consumes it.

**References**

- <https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr36/>
- <https://unicode.org/reports/tr9/>

<a id="mcp052"></a>

### MCP052 · Two servers expose a tool with the same name

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** scan · **Slug** `mcp052-two-servers-expose-a-tool-with-the-same-name`

The same tool name is contributed by more than one server, so the model cannot tell them apart.

**Why it matters**

Tool names are the model's whole vocabulary for choosing an action. When two servers provide `read_file`, a malicious server can shadow the trusted one — the classic tool-poisoning setup — and which one wins is left to client ordering, not to intent.

**Fix**

Namespace tool names per server (e.g. `github_read_file`), and remove the redundant server.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices>

## schema

<a id="mcp060"></a>

### MCP060 · Tool parameter accepts unconstrained input

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** tool · **Slug** `mcp060-tool-parameter-accepts-unconstrained-input`

A sensitive parameter is a free-form string with no enum, pattern, format, or length limit.

**Why it matters**

The schema is the model's only specification of what a value may be. For parameters that become a path, a URL, or a command, the absence of a constraint is an invitation to pass anything — and it removes the client-side validation that would otherwise reject a traversal or an injected flag.

**Fix**

Constrain the parameter: an `enum` for known choices, `format`/`pattern` for paths and URLs, `maxLength`, and `additionalProperties: false` on the object.

**References**

- <https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/>

<a id="mcp061"></a>

### MCP061 · Destructive tool is not annotated as destructive

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** tool · **Slug** `mcp061-destructive-tool-is-not-annotated-as-destructive`

A tool that changes or destroys state carries no destructiveHint, so clients cannot gate it.

**Why it matters**

MCP tool annotation hints are what a client uses to decide whether to ask the human first. A tool named `delete_branch` that declares no hints is indistinguishable from a read-only one to any client that relies on annotations, and a tool marked `readOnlyHint: true` while deleting data actively misleads the review.

**Fix**

Declare `annotations: { destructiveHint: true, readOnlyHint: false }`, and keep the name accurate.

**References**

- <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools#tool-annotations>

<a id="mcp062"></a>

### MCP062 · Tool input schema is malformed

**Severity** `low` · **Applies to** tool · **Slug** `mcp062-tool-input-schema-is-malformed`

inputSchema is missing, is not an object, or has the wrong shape for properties/required.

**Why it matters**

A malformed schema is not merely untidy: clients that generate a tool definition from it may fall back to accepting anything, and clients that validate will fail at call time — after the user has already approved the action.

**Fix**

Publish a valid JSON Schema object with `type: "object"`, a `properties` map, and `required` as an array of names.

**References**

- <https://json-schema.org/>

## configuration

<a id="mcp070"></a>

### MCP070 · Server entry has an unusable shape

**Severity** `low` · **Applies to** warning · **Slug** `mcp070-server-entry-has-an-unusable-shape`

A server entry is missing a required field or has a field of the wrong type.

**Why it matters**

Clients disagree about how strict they are: some reject the whole file, others drop the server silently. Either way the developer believes a capability exists that does not, or gets an error with no location.

**Fix**

Fix the entry shape; the message names the field the loader could not use.

<a id="mcp072"></a>

### MCP072 · Config file could not be parsed

**Severity** `medium` · **Applies to** error · **Slug** `mcp072-config-file-could-not-be-parsed`

A config or descriptor file is unreadable or is not valid JSON/JSONC.

**Why it matters**

An unparsable config is unaudited: this tool could not inspect it, and the client will either refuse to start or fall back to defaults. Silence here would look like a clean scan, which is the one outcome a security report must never fabricate.

**Fix**

Fix the syntax error. mcpvet accepts comments and trailing commas, so a failure is a real defect.

## Adding a rule

Rules live in `src/rules/<category>.js` and export a `Rule` object. `src/rules/index.js` validates the whole set at import time: a duplicate id, an unknown severity, a missing rationale, or a `check` that is not a function is a hard error, not a warning. `test/rules.test.js` requires a positive *and* a negative case per rule — a rule that only ever fires is as much a bug as one that never fires.
